title: felicitous / fortuitous / gratuitous
core: Three formal four-syllable adjectives that end in the same *-itous* and all comment on how something came about — but on three different axes: whether it was well-judged, whether anyone planned it, and whether anything justified it. The shape is the trap; the Latin roots are unrelated (*felix* happy, *fors* chance, *gratis* free). One is praise, one is neutral report, one is an accusation.
exam_note: Sentence-equivalence traps swap **fortuitous** into a slot that rewards a deliberate good choice (**felicitous**) — and lean on the popular "luckily accidental" reading when the GRE is testing plain *unplanned*.

words.nuance: The only one that credits someone's judgment — a person chose well and you admire the choice. It attaches to craft: phrasing, metaphors, titles, the timing of a toast. Its secondary "happy, fortunate" sense still carries no idea of accident.

Reports only that nobody arranged it. Silent on whether the result was good and silent on skill — a fortuitous meeting was chosen by no one, where a felicitous one was arranged with taste. On the exam, read it as *unplanned* and let the sentence supply the luck.

The only accusation, and it's aimed at the doer: the excess was unprovoked and faintly enjoyed. Not chance and not aptness but warrant — nothing called for it. Watch the collocations that give it away: gratuitous violence, cruelty, insult, swipe. In legal prose it means merely *free of charge*, no blame attached.
